Transfert est le podcast d'histoires vra: Transfert is the true-story podcast from Slate.fr, the French spin-off of the American magazine, launched in February 2009 by Jean-Marie Colombani, Jacques Attali, Éric Leser, Johan Hufnagel and Éric Le Boucher. An outlet known for analysis and catchy headlines — its proud trademark — whose English name means both a "writing tablet" and "to criticise harshly". Which makes it all the more delicious that it produced one of the gentlest podcasts in France.
Lancé en 2016, Transfert fête ses dix an: Launched in 2016, Transfert celebrates its tenth anniversary without changing its formula: every week, one person tells a true story, the moment their life tipped over. No journalist on air, no questions, no context at the start: a voice, an edit, a sound bed, twenty to thirty minutes. Behind it, a real team — Sarah Koskievic and Benjamin Saeptem Hours running the show and its editorial production, the latter also composing the music.
Une histoire vraie brute, c'est ennuyeux: A raw true story is boring: people digress, repeat themselves, forget. Transfert's talent is taking hours of recording and turning them into twenty-five minutes where every sentence moves forward. The journalist has disappeared from the picture, not from the work — and that's harder than asking questions.
En 2016, personne ne faisait ça en Franc: In 2016, nobody was doing this in France: twenty-five minutes of testimony with no expert, no panel, no debate. It was a gamble. It has become a reference for French narrative podcasting, and much of what has been made since owes it something.
Aucun épisode n'en suppose un autre : on: No episode assumes another: you can start anywhere. Lolo's advice — pick one at random, definitely don't read the summary, put on headphones and do nothing else. Not in the background while tidying up. And preferably not on the metro.
Lolo portait le verdict, non sans avoir: Lolo delivered the verdict, not without being outed from the start: he cried on the train for twenty-eight minutes, and passengers changed carriages. So Alex investigated by playing "Slate or Gorafi" — a real Slate headline or a fake one? — the better to salute the paradox: an analysis outlet co-founded by Jacques Attali whose flagship concept consists of keeping quiet and listening to someone. The underlying conclusion is unambiguous: Transfert has held for ten years on a simple idea, that people are more interesting than the experts who talk about people, and executes it with rare care.
Les réserves sont réelles, et Lolo les a: The reservations are real, and Lolo voiced them himself. Nothing is verified: a person tells their version, with no counterpoint — the pact says "story", but the listener hears "true story" and believes everything. Selection pushes towards the most spectacular lives, to the point of suggesting everyone has lived through a turning point, when most people have mainly lived through a mortgage. The sound design, magnificent, is also directive: the music tells you when to be sad, even when the story would suffice. And anonymity, needed to protect witnesses, makes any verification impossible — a price to pay knowingly. For storytelling with counterpoint and archives, see Affaires sensibles, reviewed in our episode 49; for intimate first-person stories, Émotions, our episode 11.
